chunks.title: Comparative Analysis — Vata vs. Pitta vs. Kapha Doshas
chunks.content: A comparative overview of the three doshas highlights their distinct physiological functions, elements, and attributes: 1. Elemental Makeup: Vata is Ether + Air; Pitta is Fire + Water; Kapha is Water + Earth. 2. Primary Role: Vata is Kinetic/Catabolic (movement, nerve transmission, excretion); Pitta is Metabolic/Transformative (digestion, enzymatic reactions, heat); Kapha is Structural/Anabolic (cohesion, growth, lubrication). 3. Thermal Nature: Vata is Cold (Sheeta); Pitta is Hot (Ushna); Kapha is Cold (Sheeta). 4. Moisture Nature: Vata is Dry (Ruksha); Pitta is Lightly Oily (Sasneha); Kapha is Very Oily/Unctuous (Snigdha). 5. Weight/Density: Vata is Light (Laghu); Pitta is Light (Laghu); Kapha is Heavy (Guru). 6. Primary Seat in Body: Vata resides primarily in the colon (Pakwashaya), pelvis, and bones; Pitta resides in the small intestine (Grahani), stomach, and liver; Kapha resides in the chest (Uras), throat, and head.
chunks.source: Ashtanga Hridaya — Sutrasthana (Educational Translation)

chunks.title: Classical Ayurveda Literature — The Brihat Trayi (Great Triad)
chunks.content: The authoritative corpus of classical Ayurveda is anchored in the 'Brihat Trayi' (The Great Three Treatises): 1. Charaka Samhita: Primarily attributed to Acharya Charaka, focusing predominantly on Kaya Chikitsa (internal medicine), foundational philosophy, epistemology, etiology (Nidana), and therapeutics. Emphasizes mind-body balance and lifestyle. 2. Sushruta Samhita: Attributed to Acharya Sushruta, known globally as the pioneer of surgery (Shalya Chikitsa); details surgical procedures, rhinoplasty, anatomical dissections (Sharira), surgical instruments, and trauma management. 3. Ashtanga Hridaya / Ashtanga Sangraha: Composed by Acharya Vagbhata; brilliantly synthesizes and condenses the core teachings of both Charaka and Sushruta into poetic, memorable Sanskrit verses covering all eight clinical branches of Ayurveda (Ashtanga Ayurveda).
chunks.source: History of Indian Medicine and AYUSH Research
chunks.section: Classical Heritage: Overview of Brihat Trayi

chunks.title: The Eight Clinical Branches — Ashtanga Ayurveda
chunks.content: Ayurveda traditionally encompasses eight specialized medical branches, termed Ashtanga Ayurveda: 1. Kaya Chikitsa: Internal medicine and general systemic disorders. 2. Shalya Tantra: Surgical techniques, wound care, and foreign body extraction. 3. Shalakya Tantra: Disorders of the ear, nose, throat, eyes, and oral cavity (supraclavicular medicine). 4. Kaumarabhritya: Pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology. 5. Agada Tantra: Toxicology, poisons, and environmental hazards. 6. Rasayana Tantra: Rejuvenation, geriatrics, longevity science, and cellular vitalization. 7. Vajikarana Tantra: Virility, reproductive health, and healthy progeny. 8. Bhuta Vidya (Graha Chikitsa): Psychotherapy and psycho-spiritual health. Together, these branches provided a comprehensive healthcare matrix in classical India.
chunks.source: Ministry of AYUSH — Classical Ayurvedic Frameworks
chunks.section: Introduction to the Eight Branches of Ayurveda

chunks.title: What is Ayurveda — Origin and Definition
chunks.content: Ayurveda is one of the world's oldest holistic healing systems, originating in the Indian subcontinent more than 3,000 to 5,000 years ago. The word 'Ayurveda' is derived from two Sanskrit roots: 'Ayu' meaning 'life' or 'longevity', and 'Veda' meaning 'knowledge' or 'sacred science'. Together, Ayurveda translates to 'The Science of Life'. According to classical texts such as the Charaka Samhita, health (Swastha) is not merely the absence of disease, but a state of dynamic equilibrium between body, mind, spirit, and environment: 'Samadosha Samagnischa Samadhatu Malakriya Prasannatmendriyamanah Swastha Iti Abhidhiyate' (Sushruta Samhita). Health is maintained when doshas, metabolic fire (Agni), bodily tissues (Dhatus), and excretory functions (Malas) are in balanced proportion, and soul, senses, and mind are at peace.
chunks.source: CCRAS - Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences
chunks.section: Ayurveda: The Science of Life and Well-being

chunks.title: Panchamahabhuta — The Five Great Elements
chunks.content: Ayurveda posits that all matter in the universe, including the human body, is composed of the five fundamental elements known as Panchamahabhutas: 1. Akasha (Space/Ether): characterized by non-resistance, omnipresence, lightness, and subtle sound; forms body cavities and conduits. 2. Vayu (Air): characterized by mobility, dryness, coolness, and lightness; governs biological movement, nerve impulses, and breathing. 3. Tejas/Agni (Fire): characterized by heat, luminosity, transformation, and sharpness; governs digestion, metabolism, sight, and body temperature. 4. Jala/Apas (Water): characterized by fluidity, liquidity, coolness, and cohesion; provides lubrication, cytoplasm, plasma, and bodily secretions. 5. Prithvi (Earth): characterized by stability, heaviness, density, and structure; forms bones, muscles, cartilage, and teeth. Every physical substance contains all five elements in varying proportions, with one or two predominating.
chunks.source: Ministry of AYUSH — Fundamentals of Ayurveda Guidelines
chunks.section: Chapter 1: Cosmic Elements and Biological Composition

chunks.title: Tridosha Theory — Overview of the Three Bio-energies
chunks.content: The Tridosha theory is the cornerstone of Ayurvedic physiology and pathology. The five elements combine in pairs to form three dynamic bio-energetic forces called Doshas: Vata, Pitta, and Kapha. The word 'Dosha' etymologically means 'that which can become vitiated or imbalanced', but in their balanced state (Samyavastha), they sustain all physiological functions: 1. Vata (composed of Space and Air) governs all biological movement, circulation, respiration, and nervous system impulses. 2. Pitta (composed of Fire and Water) governs all metabolic transformation, biochemical reactions, digestion, body heat, and cognitive clarity. 3. Kapha (composed of Water and Earth) governs physical structure, cellular cohesion, lubrication, immunity, stability, and emotional grounding. Each individual possesses a unique proportional baseline of these three doshas formed at conception, known as Prakriti.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia & Fundamentals (AYUSH)
chunks.section: Principles of Tridosha and Biological Balance

chunks.title: Vata Dosha — Characteristics, Functions, and Qualities
chunks.content: Vata Dosha is primarily composed of Akasha (Space) and Vayu (Air). It is considered the leader of the doshas ('Pittu pangu, kapha pangu...') because Pitta and Kapha are mobile only when carried by Vata. The traditional qualities (Gunas) of Vata are: Ruksha (dry), Laghu (light), Sheeta (cold), Khara (rough), Sukshma (subtle), and Chala (mobile). Functions of balanced Vata include initiation of natural urges, sensory perception, motor activity, speech, cellular division, heart rhythm, and mental alertness. When Vata is aggravated, manifestations include dry skin, constipation, flatulence, insomnia, nervousness, cold extremities, and musculoskeletal stiffness. Vata increases during autumn, late afternoon (2 PM to 6 PM), after digestion, and in the elder stage of life.
chunks.source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana (Educational Edition)

chunks.title: Pitta Dosha — Characteristics, Functions, and Qualities
chunks.content: Pitta Dosha is primarily composed of Tejas (Fire) and Jala (Water). It governs all thermogenesis, biochemical transformations, enzymatic action, and cognitive processing. The classical qualities (Gunas) of Pitta are: Sasneha (slightly unctuous/oily), Teekshna (sharp/penetrating), Ushna (hot), Laghu (light), Visra (fleshy odor), Sara (flowing/spreading), and Drava (liquid). Functions of balanced Pitta include robust digestion (Pachana), optical visual acuity, maintenance of normal body temperature, healthy complexion, intelligence, courage, and discernment. When Pitta is vitiated, manifestations include acid indigestion, heartburn, excessive sweating, inflammatory conditions, skin irritations, irritability, and loose stools. Pitta naturally peaks during summer, midday (10 AM to 2 PM), midnight, mid-digestion, and youth.
chunks.source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana (Educational Edition)

chunks.title: Kapha Dosha — Characteristics, Functions, and Qualities
chunks.content: Kapha Dosha is formed from Jala (Water) and Prithvi (Earth). It provides structural foundation, anatomical stability, tissue lubrication, and biological resilience (Bala). The classical qualities (Gunas) of Kapha are: Guru (heavy), Sheeta (cold), Mridu (soft), Snigdha (unctuous/oily), Madhura (sweet), Sthira (stable), and Pichchila (slimy/cohesive). Functions of balanced Kapha include lubrication of joints (Sandhibandha), immunity (Ojas generation), cellular cohesion, strength, patience, forgiving temperament, and endurance. When Kapha is elevated, symptoms include lethargy, excessive sleepiness, slow digestion, congestion, heaviness, fluid retention, and weight gain. Kapha naturally peaks in late winter and spring, in the morning (6 AM to 10 AM), evening (6 PM to 10 PM), and childhood.
chunks.source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana (Educational Edition)

chunks.title: Prakriti and Vikriti — Constitution vs. Imbalance
chunks.content: In Ayurveda, Prakriti refers to an individual's unique biological constitution established at the moment of conception (Shukra-Shonita Samyoga), influenced by parental genetics, maternal diet and mental state, and seasonal factors. Prakriti remains essentially constant throughout a person's lifetime and determines physical build, digestive tendency, psychological disposition, and disease vulnerability. The primary categories are Vataja, Pittaja, Kaphaja, dual-dosha combinations (Vata-Pitta, Pitta-Kapha, Vata-Kapha), and balanced tridoshic (Samadosha). In contrast, Vikriti denotes the current state of doshic imbalance resulting from inappropriate diet, lifestyle, climate changes, psychological stress, or age. The educational objective of Ayurveda is to recognize deviations from one's baseline Prakriti and restore balance through gentle dietary and lifestyle adjustments.
chunks.source: CCRAS — Clinical & Research Methodology in Ayurveda
chunks.section: Concept of Deha Prakriti and Assessment Frameworks

chunks.title: Agni — The Digestive and Metabolic Fire
chunks.content: Agni represents the biological fire responsible for digestion, absorption, assimilation, and transformation of food and experiences. According to Charaka, 'Rogah sarve api mande agnau'—all somatic diseases originate from impaired Agni. Ayurveda describes thirteen types of Agni: 1. Jatharagni (the master digestive fire in the gastrointestinal tract); 2. Five Bhutagnis (elemental metabolic fires transforming nutrients according to the 5 elements); 3. Seven Dhatvagnis (tissue-specific metabolic fires responsible for synthesizing each of the seven bodily tissues). There are four clinical states of Jatharagni: Sama Agni (balanced digestion), Vishama Agni (irregular, fluctuating digestion associated with Vata), Tikshna Agni (hyperactive, sharp digestion associated with Pitta), and Manda Agni (sluggish, slow digestion associated with Kapha). Protecting Agni is the primary preventative directive in Ayurveda.
chunks.source: Charaka Samhita — Chikitsasthana (Educational Edition)

chunks.title: Ama — Endogenous Metabolic Toxins
chunks.content: Ama literally translates to 'unripe', 'undigested', or 'uncooked'. When digestive fire (Jatharagni) is compromised, ingested food is not properly metabolized. Instead, it ferments and produces an unassimilated, foul-smelling, sticky metabolic byproduct called Ama. Ama clogs the micro-circulatory channels (Srotas), interferes with cellular communication, and combines with vitiated doshas to initiate pathology (Samadosha). Classical signs of Ama accumulation include: feeling of heaviness (Gaurava), chronic fatigue and lassitude, coated tongue with bad breath, constipation or irregular sticky stools, loss of appetite, and mental fogginess. Traditional management focuses on Deepana (stimulating digestive fire) and Pachana (metabolizing Ama through light diet, warm water, and digestive spices like dry ginger and cumin).
chunks.source: Ashtanga Hridaya — Sutrasthana (Educational Translation)

chunks.title: Sapta Dhatus — The Seven Bodily Tissues
chunks.content: Ayurveda describes human anatomy in terms of seven structural and physiological tissues termed Sapta Dhatus, which nourish each other sequentially: 1. Rasa (Plasma/lymph): sustains hydration and nutrition ('Preenana'); 2. Rakta (Blood/erythrocytes): imparts color, vitality, and oxygenation ('Jeevana'); 3. Mamsa (Muscle tissue): envelops bone and executes movement ('Lepana'); 4. Meda (Adipose/fat tissue): lubricates body parts and buffers temperature ('Sneha'); 5. Asthi (Bone tissue): provides physical framework and protects vital organs ('Dharana'); 6. Majja (Bone marrow and nervous tissue): fills bone cavities and facilitates nerve conduction ('Poorana'); 7. Shukra (Reproductive tissue/vital essence): enables fertility and cellular regeneration ('Garbhotpadana'). The refined subtle essence of all seven healthy Dhatus is called Ojas.
chunks.source: Sushruta Samhita — Sharirasthana (Educational Edition)

chunks.title: Srotas, Malas, and Ojas — Channels, Wastes, and Vital Immunity
chunks.content: Three foundational physiological concepts in Ayurveda complete systemic understanding: 1. Srotas (Micro and Macro Channels): conduits through which nutrients, waste, and bio-energies circulate. Classical texts identify major internal systems including Pranavaha (respiratory), Annavaha (digestive), and Udakavaha (fluid regulation) srotas. 2. Malas (Excretory Metabolic Byproducts): bodily wastes whose prompt excretion maintains systemic purity: Purisha (feces), Mutra (urine), and Sweda (perspiration). Balanced waste formation and evacuation are vital for preventing auto-intoxication. 3. Ojas: the purest, most refined biological essence derived from the completion of tissue synthesis (Dhatu Paka). Ojas represents primary systemic immunity (Vyadhikshamatva), cellular resilience, sensory clarity, and radiant vitality.
chunks.source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana (Educational Edition)

chunks.title: Tulsi (Holy Basil) — Ocimum sanctum
chunks.content: Tulsi (Holy Basil / Ocimum sanctum), revered in India as the 'Queen of Herbs', holds supreme status in Ayurvedic pharmacology. Traditional attributes: Rasa (Taste): Katu (pungent), Tikta (bitter); Guna (Qualities): Laghu (light), Ruksha (dry), Teekshna (piercing); Virya (Potency): Ushna (hot); Vipaka (Post-digestive effect): Katu (pungent); Dosha effect: Pacifies Vata and Kapha, slightly increases Pitta if used in excess. Parts traditionally used: Leaves, seeds, and root. Traditional uses: Alleviates respiratory disorders (Kasa, Shwasa), enhances Pranavaha srotas clarity, boosts digestive warmth (Deepana), and relieves microbial distress (Krimihara). Modern Scientific Observations: Clinical trials indicate adaptogenic, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and antioxidant properties due to eugenol, rosmarinic acid, and carvacrol compounds.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol II

chunks.title: Ashwagandha (Indian Ginseng) — Withania somnifera
chunks.content: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), traditionally known for bestowing 'the strength of a horse' ('Ashwa' = horse, 'Gandha' = scent), is classified as a premier Medhya Rasayana (cognitive and rejuvenating tonic) and Balya (strength enhancer). Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Kashaya (astringent), Madhura (sweet); Guna: Laghu (light), Snigdha (unctuous); Virya: Ushna (hot); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Strongly pacifies Vata and Kapha. Parts used: Dried roots. Traditional uses: Deeply rejuvenates nervous system (Majja Dhatu), supports restful sleep (Nidrajanana), enhances physical endurance, combats debility, and bolsters reproductive vitality (Shukrala). Modern Scientific Observations: Extensive studies corroborate withanolides as active compounds promoting stress reduction, lowering serum cortisol levels, supporting cognitive function, and modulating neuro-protective pathways.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

chunks.title: Amalaki / Amla (Indian Gooseberry) — Phyllanthus emblica
chunks.content: Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica / Emblica officinalis) is acclaimed as one of the most potent rejuvenative fruits in Ayurveda and the central constituent of Chyawanprash. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Possesses 5 of the 6 tastes—predominantly Amla (sour), with Kashaya (astringent), Madhura (sweet), Tikta (bitter), and Katu (pungent); only lacking Lavana (salty); Guna: Guru (heavy), Ruksha (dry), Sheeta (cooling); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Tridosha Shamaka (balances all three doshas, especially pacifies Pitta due to cold potency and sweet post-digestive effect). Parts used: Fresh and dried fruit pericarps. Traditional uses: Rasayana (longevity promoter), Chakshushya (preserves eyesight), Hridya (supports cardiac strength), and promotes hair growth. Modern Scientific Observations: One of nature's densest sources of bioavailable ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), rich in ellagitannins (emblicanin A and B) demonstrating remarkable hepatoprotective, cardioprotective, and antioxidant activity.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

chunks.title: Haridra / Turmeric — Curcuma longa
chunks.content: Haridra (Curcuma longa) is celebrated in classical texts for its purifying, anti-inflammatory, and complexion-enhancing qualities. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Katu (pungent); Guna: Ruksha (dry), Laghu (light); Virya: Ushna (hot); Vipaka: Katu (pungent); Dosha effect: Pacifies Kapha and Vata; detoxifies Rakta (blood) and Pitta when used appropriately. Parts used: Dried rhizomes. Traditional uses: Varnya (promotes luminous complexion), Vishaghna (antitoxic/purifying), Kushtaghna (supports skin health), and Pramehahara (supports healthy carbohydrate metabolism). Modern Scientific Observations: Curcuminoids, especially curcumin, are extensively documented in modern biomedical literature for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, wound-healing, and antimicrobial efficacy. Piperine (from black pepper / Maricha) enhances its bioavailability substantially.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

chunks.title: Neem (Nimba) — Azadirachta indica
chunks.content: Nimba (Azadirachta indica), termed 'Arishta' (reliever of sickness), is renowned for its intense bitterness and systemic cooling properties. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Kashaya (astringent); Guna: Laghu (light), Ruksha (dry); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Katu (pungent); Dosha effect: Highly pacifies Pitta and Kapha; can aggravate Vata if used excessively. Parts used: Bark, leaves, seeds, and root. Traditional uses: Blood purification (Raktashodhaka), management of skin imbalances (Kushta), fever alleviation (Jwarahara), oral hygiene (Danta Dhavana), and antimicrobial cleansing (Krimighna). Modern Scientific Observations: Nimbin, nimbidin, and azadirachtin provide documented antibacterial, antifungal, anti-ulcer, and anti-inflammatory properties.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol II

chunks.title: Brahmi / Bacopa — Bacopa monnieri
chunks.content: Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri), named after Brahma the cosmic creator, is the premier Medhya Rasayana (cognitive and intellect rejuvenator). Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Kashaya (astringent), Madhura (sweet); Guna: Laghu (light); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Tridosha Shamaka, particularly soothes Pitta and Vata. Parts used: Whole aerial plant. Traditional uses: Enhances Dhi (comprehension), Dhriti (retention), and Smriti (recall); soothes central nervous system agitation, promotes mental tranquility, and improves sleep quality. Modern Scientific Observations: Bacosides A and B cross the blood-brain barrier, facilitating synaptic neurotransmission, promoting cerebral blood flow, and scavenging reactive oxygen species in the hippocampus.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol II

chunks.title: Triphala — The Classical Three-Fruit Synergy
chunks.content: Triphala ('three fruits') is the quintessential polyherbal formulation of classical Ayurveda, consisting of equal parts dried fruit pericarps of: 1. Haritaki (Terminalia chebula): balances Vata; 2. Bibhitaki (Terminalia bellirica): balances Kapha; 3. Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica): balances Pitta. Combined, Triphala is a master Tridoshic regulator. Traditional attributes: Contains 5 tastes (all except salty); predominantly Kashaya-Tikta with sweet aftertaste; moderate thermal action. Traditional uses: Anulomana (gentle non-habit-forming bowel regulator and carminative), Chakshushya (ocular health), Deepana-Pachana (kindles Agni, clears Ama), and Rasayana (cellular re-nourishment). Modern Scientific Observations: Rich in gallic acid, ellagic acid, and chebulic acid; clinically noted for regulating gut microbiome balance, supporting colonic motility, providing antioxidant defense, and exhibiting prebiotic properties.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Formulary of India (AFI) Part I

chunks.title: Guduchi / Giloy — Tinospora cordifolia
chunks.content: Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia), traditionally called 'Amrita' (the heavenly nectar of immortality), is one of the most revered immunomodulatory herbs in Ayurveda. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Tikta (bitter), Kashaya (astringent); Guna: Guru (heavy), Snigdha (unctuous); Virya: Ushna (hot); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Balances all three doshas (Tridoshahara). Parts used: Mature stems. Traditional uses: Rasayana, Deepana, Jwaraghna (dispels chronic fevers), Raktashodhaka (purifies blood), and enhances overall Vyadhikshamatva (vital natural immunity). Modern Scientific Observations: Modern pharmacological evaluations show rich presence of tinosporide, cordifolioside, and diterpenoid lactones that stimulate macrophage activity, enhance humoral immunity, and protect liver and renal cellular integrity.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

chunks.title: Yashtimadhu / Licorice (Jyeshthamadh / Mulethi) — Glycyrrhiza glabra
chunks.content: Yashtimadhu (Glycyrrhiza glabra), popularly known in Marathi as Jyeshthamadh and in Hindi as Mulethi, is the premier soothing demulcent and respiratory herb in Ayurvedic medicine. Traditional attributes: Rasa: Madhura (sweet); Guna: Guru (heavy), Snigdha (unctuous); Virya: Sheeta (cooling); Vipaka: Madhura (sweet); Dosha effect: Pacifies Vata and Pitta, and liquefies vitiated Kapha without aggravating it. Parts used: Dried roots and stolons. Traditional uses: Kanthya (improves voice and relieves sore throat), Kasa-hara (relieves dry and irritative cough / khokla), Shwasa-hara (eases bronchial spasms), and Vranaropaka (heals mucosal ulcerations). Classical home remedies pair Yashtimadhu powder with honey, ghee, or warm water for immediate throat soothing and cough alleviation. Modern Scientific Observations: Rich in glycyrrhizin, isoliquiritigenin, and flavonoids exhibiting documented expectorant, antitussive, anti-inflammatory, and mucosal-protective activities.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) Part I, Vol I

chunks.title: Sitopaladi Churna — Classical Formulation for Cough, Cold & Respiratory Balance
chunks.content: Sitopaladi Churna is one of the most famous classical polyherbal formulations described in the Sharangadhara Samhita and Charaka Samhita for the management of respiratory ailments (Pranavaha Sroto-roga). Constituents: 1. Sitopala (Rock candy / Mishri) — 16 parts; 2. Vamshalochana (Bamboo manna) — 8 parts; 3. Pippali (Long pepper / Piper longum) — 4 parts; 4. Ela (Cardamom / Elettaria cardamomum) — 2 parts; 5. Twak (Cinnamon / Cinnamomum zeylanicum) — 1 part. Traditional attributes: Balances Kapha and Pitta doshas; Deepana (digestive stimulant), Kasahara (effective against both dry and productive cough / khokla), and Jwarahara (relieves low-grade fever associated with cold). Traditional usage: Taken traditionally with honey and warm ghee or warm milk. Modern Scientific Observations: Piperine from Pippali enhances systemic bioavailability and macrophage phagocytosis, while essential oils from cardamom and cinnamon exert natural bronchodilatory and antimicrobial effects.
chunks.source: Ayurvedic Formulary of India (AFI) Part I

chunks.title: Dinacharya — The Ayurvedic Daily Regimen
chunks.content: Dinacharya refers to the sacred daily routine prescribed by Ayurveda to align circadian physiology with natural solar and planetary rhythms. Traditional daily practices include: 1. Brahma Muhurta: Waking approximately 48 to 96 minutes before sunrise, when atmospheric Vata and Sattvic clarity predominate. 2. Saucha: Evacuation of natural bowel and bladder urges. 3. Danta Dhavana & Jihwa Nirlekhana: Cleaning teeth with herbal powders (Neem, Babool) and gently scraping the tongue from back to front with copper or stainless steel scraper to remove overnight toxic film (Ama). 4. Gandusha / Kavala: Oil pulling with warm sesame or coconut oil for 5 to 15 minutes to strengthen teeth, gums, and oral microbiota. 5. Netra Prakshalana & Nasya: Washing eyes with cool water or triphala wash, followed by 1-2 drops of warm sesame oil or Anu Taila in each nostril to lubricate nasal pathways. 6. Abhyanga: Warm oil self-massage before bathing to soothe Vata, nourish skin, and enhance circulation. 7. Vyayama: Moderate physical exercise (up to half of one's capacity, indicated by mild perspiration on forehead and nose). 8. Snana: Cleansing warm bath.
chunks.source: Ashtanga Hridaya — Sutrasthana (Educational Translation)

chunks.title: Ritucharya — Seasonal Regimen and Biological Adjustments
chunks.content: Ritucharya is the systematic adjustment of diet, clothing, and activity according to the six seasons (Ritus) recognized in traditional Indian climatology: 1. Shishira (Late Winter): strong Agni; hearty, nourishing, unctuous foods are suitable. 2. Vasanta (Spring): environmental warming liquefies accumulated Kapha; light, easily digestible foods, barley, honey, and dry massage (Udvartana) are recommended to prevent congestion. 3. Grishma (Summer): scorching sun depletes bodily moisture and spikes Pitta; cooling, sweet, liquid foods, hydration, and avoiding intense midday sun are advised. 4. Varsha (Monsoon): dampened digestive fire requires light, warm, sour-salty foods and boiled water to prevent Vata accumulation and microbial distress. 5. Sharad (Autumn): sudden solar heat triggers Pitta vitiation; bitter (Tikta), sweet (Madhura), and astringent (Kashaya) herbs and foods with ghee are traditionally taken. 6. Hemanta (Early Winter): robust digestion permits rich, warming, sweet foods. Adapting to seasonal transitions prevents cyclical sickness.
chunks.source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana (Educational Edition)

chunks.title: Ahara — Ayurvedic Dietary Principles and the Six Tastes (Shad Rasa)
chunks.content: Ayurveda regards Ahara (food) as the foremost pillar of longevity ('Mahabheshaja' or the greatest medicine). Food is classified according to six fundamental tastes (Shad Rasa): 1. Madhura (Sweet): nourishing, builds tissues, pacifies Vata and Pitta, increases Kapha. 2. Amla (Sour): stimulates appetite and digestion, pacifies Vata, increases Pitta and Kapha. 3. Lavana (Salty): retains moisture, aids digestion, pacifies Vata, increases Pitta and Kapha. 4. Katu (Pungent/Spicy): clears sinuses and stimulates circulation, pacifies Kapha, increases Vata and Pitta. 5. Tikta (Bitter): detoxifying, purifying, cooling, pacifies Pitta and Kapha, increases Vata. 6. Kashaya (Astringent): drying, heals tissues, pacifies Pitta and Kapha, increases Vata. A balanced meal should ideally include all six tastes in suitable proportion, eaten in a calm environment only after the previous meal has been fully digested.
chunks.source: Ministry of AYUSH — Dietary Guidelines for Swastha Vritta
chunks.section: Principles of Ayurvedic Nutrition and Gastronomy

chunks.title: Viruddha Ahara — Incompatible Food Combinations
chunks.content: Viruddha Ahara refers to food items that, when combined, processed, or consumed under improper conditions, possess mutually conflicting biological properties that disrupt digestion and induce chronic Ama formation. Classical examples of incompatible combinations include: 1. Milk combined with sour fruits, citrus, or melons (which curdles milk proteins and deranges gut fermentation); 2. Equal quantities by weight of honey and ghee (traditionally considered toxic due to conflicting thermal and chemical reactions); 3. Heating honey above 40°C / boiling honey (which creates sticky, unassimilable biochemical molecules according to Charaka); 4. Milk consumed with fish (conflicting thermal potencies: fish is hot/Ushna, milk is cold/Sheeta); 5. Eating cold, iced water immediately before, during, or after warm meals (which extinguishes Jatharagni).
chunks.source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana (Educational Edition)

chunks.title: Nidra — Sleep as the Second Pillar of Life
chunks.content: In Ayurveda, Trayopastambha refers to the three supportive pillars of life: Ahara (nutrition), Nidra (sleep), and Brahmacharya (regulated vitality and sensory moderation). Charaka declares: 'Happiness, nourishment, strength, virility, knowledge, and life itself depend upon proper sleep.' Sound sleep (Sukha Nidra) allows cellular restoration, deep tissue rejuvenation, and psychological integration of memories. Daytime sleep (Divaswapna) is generally contraindicated in adults as it sharply vitiates Kapha and Pitta and causes channel obstruction, except during severe summer heat or for convalescents and the elderly. Sleeping on the left side (Vamkukshi) after light digestion is traditionally recommended to optimize digestive fire (located on the left) and promote efficient breathing through the right nostril (Surya Nadi).

chunks.title: Yoga, Pranayama, and Meditation in Ayurvedic Health
chunks.content: Ayurveda and Yoga are sister sciences rooted in Vedic philosophy. While Yoga addresses spiritual emancipation and mental mastery through the eight limbs (Ashtanga Yoga), Ayurveda provides the physical and physiological basis for this practice. In traditional wellness, specific Asanas (postures) and Pranayama (breath regulation) balance doshas: 1. Nadi Shodhana (Alternate Nostril Breathing) balances both hemispheres, calms aggravated Vata, and centers the nervous system; 2. Sheetali and Sheetkari (Cooling Breath) pacify excess internal Pitta and cool body temperature; 3. Bhastrika and Kapalabhati stimulate sluggish Agni, expel excess mucus, and pacify heavy Kapha. Meditation (Dhyana) reduces mental Rajas (restlessness) and Tamas (inertia), fostering Sattva (pure cognitive clarity and inner peace).
